documents.title: Learning to Segment from Scribbles using Multi-scale Adversarial Attention Gates

texts.raid-human: Large, fine-grained image segmentation datasets, annotated at pixel-level, are difficult to obtain, particularly in medical imaging, where annotations also require expert knowledge. Weakly-supervised learning can train models by relying on weaker forms of annotation, such as scribbles. Here, we learn to segment using scribble annotations in an adversarial game. With unpaired segmentation masks, we train a multi-scale GAN to generate realistic segmentation masks at multiple resolutions, while we use scribbles to learn their correct position in the image. Central to the model's success is a novel attention gating mechanism, which we condition with adversarial signals to act as a shape prior, resulting in better object localization at multiple scales. Subject to adversarial conditioning, the segmentor learns attention maps that are semantic, suppress the noisy activations outside the objects, and reduce the vanishing gradient problem in the deeper layers of the segmentor. We evaluated our model on several medical (ACDC, LVSC, CHAOS) and non-medical (PPSS) datasets, and we report performance levels matching those achieved by models trained with fully annotated segmentation masks. We also demonstrate extensions in a variety of settings: semi-supervised learning; combining multiple scribble sources (a crowdsourcing scenario) and multi-task learning (combining scribble and mask supervision). We release expert-made scribble annotations for the ACDC dataset, and the code used for the experiments, at https://vios-s.github.io/multiscale-adversarial-attention-gates
texts.raid-chatgpt: This paper proposes a novel method for learning to segment objects from scribbles using multi-scale adversarial attention gates. The method leverages the power of adversarial training to generate realistic segmentations from rough scribbles. The proposed approach incorporates multi-scale attention gates to capture both local and global contextual information, improving the accuracy of the segmentation. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness. The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications and future directions of this research.
texts.raid-gpt4: This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using scribbles as input, leveraging multi-scale adversarial attention gates. The proposed method aims to address the challenges of insufficient and imprecise annotations in medical image segmentation. The model employs a multi-scale strategy to capture features at various scales and an adversarial attention mechanism to focus on challenging regions. The adversarial training strategy is used to enhance the discriminative capability of the model. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, outperforming state-of-the-art scribble-based segmentation methods. The study also shows that the model can effectively learn from scribbles and generate high-quality segmentation results, providing a promising solution for practical applications in medical image analysis.
texts.raid-llama-chat: In this paper, we propose a novel approach for image segmentation using scribbles as supervision. Our method, called Learning to Segment from Scribbles using Multi-scale Adversarial Attention Gates (LASSO), leverages the power of adversarial attention mechanisms to effectively learn from scribble annotations. Existing approaches for segmentation from scribbles often rely on simplistic heuristics or labor-intensive manual annotation of large datasets. In contrast, LASSO uses a multi-scale adversarial attention mechanism to learn a robust representation of the image that can be used for accurate segmentation. Our approach consists of two main components: a scribble encoder and a segmentation decoder. The scribble encoder maps the scribble annotations to a set of attention weights, which are then used to guide the segmentation decoder. The decoder consists of a series of convolutional layers that refine the segmentation output at multiple scales. We evaluate LASSO on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods for segmentation from scribbles. Our experiments demonstrate that LASSO is able to accurately segment objects even when the scribble annotations are noisy or incomplete. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the different components of our approach, providing insights into the role of each component in the segmentation process. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: * We propose a novel approach for image segmentation from scribbles using multi-scale adversarial attention gates. * We introduce a scribble encoder that maps scribble annotations to attention weights, which are used to guide the segmentation decoder. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of LASSO on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods for segmentation from scribbles. * We perform ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each component of our approach, providing insights into the role of each component in the segmentation process. texts.raid-claude: Large, fully-annotated datasets are the main driver of progress in medical image segmentation, but obtaining dense pixel-level labels is expensive, slow, and requires expert knowledge. Learning from scribbles — sparse, quickly drawn strokes marking a few pixels of each class — is an attractive alternative, yet scribbles carry no information about object extent or shape, so models trained on them tend to leak across boundaries and produce anatomically implausible masks. We address this by regularising a scribble-supervised segmentor with an adversarial shape prior, learned from a set of unpaired segmentation masks that need not correspond to the training images and can be reused across datasets. Rather than applying the adversarial signal only at the output, we propose multi-scale adversarial attention gates: the discriminator's assessment of shape realism is fed back into the segmentor as attention maps that modulate its features at several resolutions, progressively suppressing activations that would yield unrealistic structures while letting the sparse scribble supervision refine local detail. The resulting model is a single-stage, end-to-end trainable network with negligible inference overhead. On cardiac MRI (ACDC, LVSC), abdominal CT/MRI (CHAOS), and pedestrian parsing (PPSS) benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms strong weakly-supervised baselines and approaches fully-supervised performance while using only a small fraction of the annotation effort. We also release scribble annotations for the cardiac datasets and make our code publicly available.

documents.title: A Generalized Asymmetric Dual-front Model for Active Contours and Image Segmentation

texts.raid-human: The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front active contour models are known as a powerful and efficient way for addressing the image segmentation and domain partitioning problems. In the basic formulation of the dual-front models, the evolving contours can be considered as the interfaces of adjacent Voronoi regions. Among these dual-front models, a crucial ingredient is regarded as the geodesic metrics by which the geodesic distances and the corresponding Voronoi diagram can be estimated. In this paper, we introduce a type of asymmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the integration of the image features and a vector field derived from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of contour shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away from the target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity distributions. Moreover, the proposed dual-front model can be applied for image segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

texts.raid-claude: The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front scheme is a powerful and efficient way to carry out curve evolution for image segmentation, in which the evolving contours are taken to be the interfaces between adjacent Voronoi regions induced by geodesic distance maps. Its behaviour is therefore governed entirely by the geodesic metric used to measure curve length, which in existing formulations is built from isotropic or symmetric anisotropic image features and consequently exploits only a limited portion of the available image information. In this paper, we introduce a generalized asymmetric dual-front model whose front propagation is driven by a family of asymmetric quadratic metrics. These metrics blend several complementary cues in a single geodesic framework: edge-based anisotropy and directionality, an asymmetry term derived from the image gradient that encourages contours to align with object boundaries in a prescribed orientation, region-based homogeneity terms that exploit appearance statistics of the regions separated by the evolving curve, and a curvature-penalized component that favours smooth and regular segmentation boundaries. The resulting geodesic distance maps are computed efficiently by a variant of the fast marching method adapted to asymmetric quadratic metrics, so that each dual-front update remains inexpensive. Experiments on synthetic and natural images, including comparisons with state-of-the-art active contour approaches, show that the proposed model is accurate, robust to contour initialization and to the placement of the narrowband region, and able to handle objects with weak, blurred or partially missing boundaries as well as strong background clutter.

documents.title: Transformer Meets Convolution: A Bilateral Awareness Net-work for Semantic Segmentation of Very Fine Resolution Ur-ban Scene Images

texts.raid-human: Semantic segmentation from very fine resolution (VFR) urban scene images plays a significant role in several application scenarios including autonomous driving, land cover classification, and urban planning, etc. However, the tremendous details contained in the VFR image severely limit the potential of the existing deep learning approaches. More seriously, the considerable variations in scale and appearance of objects further deteriorate the representational capacity of those se-mantic segmentation methods, leading to the confusion of adjacent objects. Addressing such is-sues represents a promising research field in the remote sensing community, which paves the way for scene-level landscape pattern analysis and decision making. In this manuscript, we pro-pose a bilateral awareness network (BANet) which contains a dependency path and a texture path to fully capture the long-range relationships and fine-grained details in VFR images. Specif-ically, the dependency path is conducted based on the ResT, a novel Transformer backbone with memory-efficient multi-head self-attention, while the texture path is built on the stacked convo-lution operation. Besides, using the linear attention mechanism, a feature aggregation module (FAM) is designed to effectively fuse the dependency features and texture features. Extensive experiments conducted on the three large-scale urban scene image segmentation datasets, i.e., ISPRS Vaihingen dataset, ISPRS Potsdam dataset, and UAVid dataset, demonstrate the effective-ness of our BANet. Specifically, a 64.6% mIoU is achieved on the UAVid dataset.

texts.raid-claude: Semantic segmentation of very fine resolution (VFR) urban scene imagery is a fundamental task for applications such as land-cover mapping, urban planning, and change detection. However, VFR images pose two coupled difficulties: the enlarged intra-class variance and reduced inter-class variance of ground objects demand long-range contextual reasoning, while the abundance of fine structural detail—building edges, narrow roads, small vehicles—demands the preservation of precise spatial information. Conventional convolutional neural networks, constrained by the local receptive field of the convolution operator, capture global dependencies only indirectly through deep stacking and aggressive downsampling, which in turn erodes the spatial detail that VFR imagery uniquely provides. In this paper, we propose a Bilateral Awareness Network (BANet) that couples the complementary strengths of the Transformer and the convolution. BANet comprises two parallel paths: a dependency path built upon a lightweight, efficient Transformer backbone that models long-range contextual dependencies and global semantic relationships, and a texture path composed of shallow convolutional layers that retains high-resolution, fine-grained spatial and boundary detail. Because the two paths encode information of markedly different granularity and semantic level, a feature aggregation module (FAM) is designed to bridge them, employing a combination of channel attention and spatial attention to adaptively reweight and fuse the dependency and texture representations rather than merging them by naive summation or concatenation. Extensive experiments are conducted on three benchmark datasets—the ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam 2D semantic labelling datasets and the UAVid dataset. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that BANet achieves competitive or superior accuracy in comparison with state-of-the-art lightweight segmentation networks while maintaining an efficient speed–accuracy trade-off, confirming the effectiveness of jointly exploiting global dependency modelling and local texture preservation for VFR urban scene segmentation.

documents.title: Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation

texts.raid-human: The success of deep learning methods in medical image segmentation tasks heavily depends on a large amount of labeled data to supervise the training. On the other hand, the annotation of biomedical images requires domain knowledge and can be laborious. Recently, contrastive learning has demonstrated great potential in learning latent representation of images even without any label. Existing works have explored its application to biomedical image segmentation where only a small portion of data is labeled, through a pre-training phase based on self-supervised contrastive learning without using any labels followed by a supervised fine-tuning phase on the labeled portion of data only. In this paper, we establish that by including the limited label in formation in the pre-training phase, it is possible to boost the performance of contrastive learning. We propose a supervised local contrastive loss that leverages limited pixel-wise annotation to force pixels with the same label to gather around in the embedding space. Such loss needs pixel-wise computation which can be expensive for large images, and we further propose two strategies, downsampling and block division, to address the issue. We evaluate our methods on two public biomedical image datasets of different modalities. With different amounts of labeled data, our methods consistently outperform the state-of-the-art contrast-based methods and other semi-supervised learning techniques.

texts.raid-claude: The success of deep learning methods in medical image segmentation tasks usually comes at the cost of extensive labeling of the target dataset, which is expensive and time-consuming to acquire because it demands scarce expert knowledge and pixel-level annotation of volumetric scans. Contrastive learning offers a way to exploit abundant unlabeled data, but conventional formulations treat every other image as a negative sample, which is problematic in medical imaging: scans from different patients share highly consistent anatomy, so semantically identical regions are repeatedly pushed apart, and the resulting representations transfer poorly to dense prediction. In this work we propose a semi-supervised contrastive learning framework that couples supervision from a small labeled set with a label-aware contrastive objective defined at the pixel and region level. The limited annotations, together with confident pseudo-labels produced by a mean-teacher model, are used to identify positive pairs across images that belong to the same anatomical class, while a class-aware sampling strategy prevents dominant background regions from overwhelming the loss. Contrastive representation learning and segmentation training are optimized jointly rather than sequentially, so the embedding space is shaped by the downstream objective throughout training. We evaluate our method on cardiac MRI, abdominal CT, and prostate MRI segmentation benchmarks. With only 5-10% of the labels, the proposed method consistently outperforms supervised baselines and recent semi-supervised and self-supervised approaches, recovering a large fraction of fully supervised performance and yielding the largest gains for small and low-contrast structures. Ablations confirm that both label-aware positive mining and joint optimization are necessary for these improvements.

documents.title: Points2Polygons: Context-Based Segmentation from Weak Labels Using Adversarial Networks

texts.raid-human: In applied image segmentation tasks, the ability to provide numerous and precise labels for training is paramount to the accuracy of the model at inference time. However, this overhead is often neglected, and recently proposed segmentation architectures rely heavily on the availability and fidelity of ground truth labels to achieve state-of-the-art accuracies. Failure to acknowledge the difficulty in creating adequate ground truths can lead to an over-reliance on pre-trained models or a lack of adoption in real-world applications. We introduce Points2Polygons (P2P), a model which makes use of contextual metric learning techniques that directly addresses this problem. Points2Polygons performs well against existing fully-supervised segmentation baselines with limited training data, despite using lightweight segmentation models (U-Net with a ResNet18 backbone) and having access to only weak labels in the form of object centroids and no pre-training. We demonstrate this on several different small but non-trivial datasets. We show that metric learning using contextual data provides key insights for self-supervised tasks in general, and allow segmentation models to easily generalize across traditionally label-intensive domains in computer vision.

texts.raid-claude: In applied mapping problems, transferring a pretrained segmentation model to a new region or sensor almost always requires new annotations, and dense polygon labels are expensive to produce. Point labels, by contrast, are cheap: an annotator can click object centers an order of magnitude faster than they can trace boundaries. We present Points2Polygons (P2P), a model that learns instance segmentation of small, densely packed objects in overhead imagery from point supervision alone. P2P is built on the observation that the appearance of an object is strongly constrained by its local context, so a network can be taught to hallucinate plausible object extents around labeled points if it is also forced to explain the surrounding background. The model couples a context-based generator with an adversarial discriminator that compares generated segmentations against the local image evidence, together with point-consistency and count constraints that anchor each predicted instance to its annotation. This formulation requires no seed masks, no bounding boxes, and no pretrained segmentation backbone from a related domain. We evaluate P2P on overhead imagery of built structures and agricultural objects across several geographies and ground sample distances, and show that it recovers object footprints with quality approaching fully supervised baselines while using annotations that are substantially cheaper to collect, and that it degrades gracefully as point placement becomes noisy or off-center. We further show that P2P transfers to previously unseen regions given only a small set of points from the target domain, making it practical for rapid adaptation of mapping pipelines to new areas of interest.

documents.title: Medical Image Segmentation with Limited Supervision: A Review of Deep Network Models

texts.raid-human: Despite the remarkable performance of deep learning methods on various tasks, most cutting-edge models rely heavily on large-scale annotated training examples, which are often unavailable for clinical and health care tasks. The labeling costs for medical images are very high, especially in medical image segmentation, which typically requires intensive pixel/voxel-wise labeling. Therefore, the strong capability of learning and generalizing from limited supervision, including a limited amount of annotations, sparse annotations, and inaccurate annotations, is crucial for the successful application of deep learning models in medical image segmentation. However, due to its intrinsic difficulty, segmentation with limited supervision is challenging and specific model design and/or learning strategies are needed. In this paper, we provide a systematic and up-to-date review of the solutions above, with summaries and comments about the methodologies. We also highlight several problems in this field, discussed future directions observing further investigations.

texts.raid-claude: Despite the success of deep learning in medical image segmentation, the prevailing fully supervised paradigm depends on large collections of pixel- or voxel-level annotations that are costly to obtain, require scarce clinical expertise, and are frequently affected by inter-observer variability. This has motivated a rapidly expanding body of work on segmentation models that learn from limited supervision. In this review, we survey deep network models designed to operate under annotation scarcity and organize them within a unified taxonomy spanning semi-supervised learning, weakly supervised learning with image-level labels, points, scribbles and bounding boxes, self-supervised and unsupervised pre-training, transfer learning and domain adaptation, few-shot and one-shot segmentation, and learning with noisy or sparse labels. For each family, we describe the underlying assumptions and the mechanisms by which unlabeled or coarsely labeled data are exploited, including consistency regularization and perturbation-based training, pseudo-labeling and self-training, co-training and mutual learning, adversarial and generative modeling, contrastive and masked-image pre-training, class activation maps and seed-expansion strategies, anatomical priors and shape constraints, uncertainty estimation, and label-efficient data augmentation and synthesis. We further review architectural backbones ranging from encoder-decoder convolutional networks to transformer-based and hybrid designs, and discuss how recent vision foundation models and promptable segmentation are reshaping the annotation-efficiency landscape. Commonly used benchmarks across modalities such as MRI, CT, ultrasound, X-ray, histopathology and endoscopy are summarized together with evaluation protocols, and we highlight recurring methodological issues that hinder fair comparison, including inconsistent labeled-data splits, backbone mismatches, and under-reported baselines. We conclude by identifying open challenges, including robustness to domain shift, calibration and trustworthiness, class imbalance and small-lesion segmentation, volumetric and multi-modal settings, computational cost, and clinical validation, and outline directions for developing annotation-efficient segmentation methods suitable for deployment in practice.
